attributes.name: [GCP Cloud SQL SQL Server OTel] Average lock wait duration 99% rolling 30 days
attributes.description: Tracks lock contention latency on each Cloud SQL for SQL Server instance. Each 5-minute slice is good when the average lock wait duration is 500 ms or less. Total lock wait time (ms) and lock wait count come from the SQL Server-only DELTA metrics cloudsql.googleapis.com/database/sqlserver/transactions/lock_wait_time and lock_wait_count, summed across all locked_resource series. The equation A - 500 * B <= 0 is the same as total wait / wait count <= 500 ms, and a slice with no lock waits counts as good. The objective is that 99% of slices are good over a rolling 30-day window. Long average lock waits usually come from blocking chains, long transactions, missing indexes or lock escalation, and they show up as slow statements and application timeouts. Caveats: SQL Server records lock wait time when each wait completes, so a blocking chain that is still running is not counted until it clears. A long incident can appear as only a few bad slices; use the blocked-processes panels and alerts for ongoing blocking. Intentional waits, such as sp_getapplock queues or batch jobs blocking each other, can inflate the average. The 500 ms threshold is a starting point to tune per workload. This SLO does not cover latency from CPU, I/O or memory-grant pressure. It uses only SQL Server-specific metrics, so no engine marker is needed. It has no data while the instance is stopped or down and does not measure availability; instance-down alerts cover that. Cloud Monitoring data reaches Elasticsearch 3-5 minutes late, so set the SLO sync delay to at least 5m when you create it.
